critic_changes: Arc: 'The slide began when commodity prices collapsed in the 1980s' contradicted the data, which show income per person falling sharply from 1975; reworded to 'It fell from 1974, and the slide deepened when commodity prices collapsed in the 1980s' (split into its own sentence; arc stays at 6 sentences).

Arc: 'Growth returned from 2021 on copper-led mining' attributed 2021-23 growth to mining without a source covering those years; reworded so mining is credited for carrying growth through 2025, which the IMF and World Bank 2025-26 sources support.

Thread 'Commodity bust, then war': 'drifted down after 1974 as commodity prices fell' was not supported (the source dates the commodity collapse to the 1980s, and the 1975-78 fall was steep, not a drift); 'wrecked roads, power and schools' went beyond the source's 'physical and social infrastructure'; hyperinflation was not in this thread's citations. Rewrote the text to match the passages.
Thread 'Commodity bust, then war': the quote used hyphens '1996-1997 and 1998-2002'; corrected to the page's en dashes '1996–1997 and 1998–2002'.

Thread 'The copper slump of 2015–16': dropped 'a large producer' (not in the source) and specified 'in the DRC ... from August 2015' as the passage states; changed the copper quote's apostrophe to the page's curly one.
Thread 'Conflict in the east': 'disrupts trade and farming' was not in the cited passages; changed to 'disrupts economic activity' as the World Bank says.
Thread 'Copper-led mining growth': changed 'so most workers remain' to 'leaving most workers', following the source's wording rather than adding a causal claim.

since_last_year: 'higher energy prices tied to the Middle East war' was not in the cited passages; changed to 'the effects of the war in the Middle East', which the IMF passage supports. Changed 'large' to 'major' to follow the World Bank's description of the Ebola outbreak.

Tension: the cited sources describe robust or resilient growth only for 2025, not 2024, so the 2024 figure (2.7 percent) was removed. The claim that per-person growth was low 'because ... mining creates few jobs' was also removed, since it confused a jobs point with the gap between total and per-person growth. Both the population point and the jobs point are now attributed to the World Bank, and both appear in the MPO.
Headline: 'collapsed in the 1990s wars' changed to 'collapsed in the 1990s amid war'. The 1990–2001 collapse began before the 1996 war.

Checked against the source and kept: every number (1974 peak, 59.9, 1960, -8.3 for 1990–2001, 2.5 since 2002, 1.4 vs 3.6, shrinking in 2016/2019/2020, -3.1 in 2016, 2.4 in 2025) matches growth_problem and series in desk/data/COD.json. growth_story.headline: DR Congo's income per person collapsed in the 1990s amid war and has climbed slowly on mining since 2002, yet it is still below its 1960 level.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in DR Congo peaked in 1974 and is now 59.9 percent below that peak, lower even than in 1960, the first year of the record. It fell from 1974, and the slide deepened when commodity prices collapsed in the 1980s. It became a collapse in 1990–2001, when income per person shrank by 8.3 percent a year amid hyperinflation and a two-phase war. A program begun in 2001 halted hyperinflation and a peace agreement in 2002 ended the war, opening a second era: since 2002, growth has averaged 2.5 percent a year, led by a mining boom financed by foreign investors. The last decade was slower, at 1.4 percent a year against 3.6 in the decade before, as copper prices fell in 2015–16, and income per person shrank in 2016, 2019 and 2020. Growth returned from 2021 and mining, led by copper, carried it through 2025, but with conflict in the east and a fast-growing population, income per person rose 2.4 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe robust, mining-led growth in 2025, yet income per person rose only 2.4 percent that year; the World Bank notes that rapid population growth has outpaced gains in household welfare and that mining creates few jobs. And more than two decades of recovery since 2002 have not brought income per person back to its 1960 level.
